assessment: Fox Insight Table 3 reports 26 drooling-class answers in a selected set of off-period responses outside expected wearing-off questionnaire coverage. The analysis of 2,106 respondents does not measure drooling prevalence, severity or raw fig.

Among 15 interviewees with GBA-associated Parkinson disease, seven reported excessive drooling or saliva, five dry mouth and four chewing or swallowing difficulty. This is a conceptual interview figure with no source-matched fig exposure.

A companion analysis of the same November 2018 Fox Insight survey reports 57 food timing or hunger triggers and 97 eating or drinking strategies for off periods. These broad categories lack ingredient-level drooling outcomes.
The pilot used drooling as one possible enrollment complaint and evaluated instrumental airway invasion in 135 swallows from 14 Parkinson participants. No raw-fig or drooling severity effect.
COPARK uses UPDRS salivation and a distinct SCOPA-Aut drooling question, with in-cohort and paired medication-state results. The Figure 2 legend has a publisher correction. No food exposure.
One distinct anterocollis case reported reduced drooling after clinical treatment. The case uses no graded symptom outcome, control group, Parkinson diagnosis or raw-fig exposure.

The NILS study pairs 728 participants with baseline and follow-up ratings. Drooling prevalence was 37.2% and 40.1% (p=.17), and severity means were 1.53 and 1.77 (p=.12). Separate dysphagia ratings and absence of a food exposure prevent transfer.
